levels.title: 2024 songs per genre (WHERE + GROUP BY)
levels.task: Stellar Sound wants a quick snapshot of last year. For songs whose release_date is in 2024 only, show genre and song_count = COUNT(*). GROUP BY genre. ORDER BY song_count high to low, then genre A–Z.
levels.initialCode: -- SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS song_count FROM top_songs WHERE release_date LIKE '2024-%' GROUP BY genre ORDER BY ...
levels.solution:
SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS song_count
FROM top_songs
WHERE release_date LIKE '2024-%'
GROUP BY genre
ORDER BY song_count DESC, genre;
levels.hintMessage: Filter first with WHERE release_date LIKE '2024-%', then GROUP BY genre. Name the count column song_count.
levels.successMessage: Nice! WHERE picks the rows first, then GROUP BY rolls them up by genre.

levels.title: Pop hits over a billion (two WHEREs with AND)
levels.task: Marketing at Stellar Sound is making a 'Pop Billionaires' poster. Show track_name, artist, and spotify_streams for songs where genre is 'Pop' AND spotify_streams is at least 1,000,000,000. ORDER BY spotify_streams high to low, then track_name A–Z.
levels.solution:
SELECT track_name, artist, spotify_streams
FROM top_songs
WHERE genre = 'Pop' AND spotify_streams >= 1000000000
ORDER BY spotify_streams DESC, track_name;
levels.hintMessage: Use AND to combine the two filters. >= keeps songs that hit exactly 1,000,000,000 too.
levels.successMessage: Great! AND keeps only rows that pass BOTH tests.

levels.title: Chart-wide stats in one row (many aggregates)
levels.task: Your boss wants one tidy summary row for the whole chart. In one SELECT, return four columns in this order: song_count = COUNT(*), total_streams = SUM(spotify_streams), avg_streams = AVG(spotify_streams), longest_song = MAX(duration_ms). No WHERE, no GROUP BY—one row, four numbers.
levels.initialCode: -- SELECT COUNT(*) AS song_count, SUM(...) AS total_streams, AVG(...) AS avg_streams, MAX(...) AS longest_song FROM top_songs;
levels.solution:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS song_count,
  SUM(spotify_streams) AS total_streams,
  AVG(spotify_streams) AS avg_streams,
  MAX(duration_ms) AS longest_song
FROM top_songs;
levels.hintMessage: You can stack aggregate functions in one SELECT. Column order matters: song_count, total_streams, avg_streams, longest_song.
levels.successMessage: Perfect! One row, four useful numbers—great for a status email.

levels.title: Pop artists: songs and total streams (WHERE + GROUP BY + 2 aggregates)
levels.task: A&R at Stellar Sound wants a Pop leaderboard. Filter to genre = 'Pop'. For each artist, show artist, song_count = COUNT(*), and total_streams = SUM(spotify_streams). GROUP BY artist. ORDER BY total_streams high to low, then artist A–Z.
levels.initialCode: -- SELECT artist, COUNT(*) AS song_count, SUM(spotify_streams) AS total_streams FROM top_songs WHERE genre = 'Pop' GROUP BY artist ORDER BY ...
levels.solution:
SELECT artist, COUNT(*) AS song_count, SUM(spotify_streams) AS total_streams
FROM top_songs
WHERE genre = 'Pop'
GROUP BY artist
ORDER BY total_streams DESC, artist;
levels.hintMessage: WHERE genre = 'Pop' runs first. Then GROUP BY artist so each row is one artist with COUNT(*) and SUM(spotify_streams).
levels.successMessage: Strong! You filtered, grouped, and stacked two aggregates in one query.

levels.title: Artists on the 2023–2024 chart (BETWEEN + GROUP BY + 2 aggregates)
levels.task: Stellar Sound is prepping a recap of the last two years. For songs with release_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2024-12-31', show artist, song_count = COUNT(*), and avg_streams = AVG(spotify_streams). GROUP BY artist. ORDER BY song_count high to low, then artist A–Z.
levels.initialCode: -- WHERE release_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2024-12-31' GROUP BY artist
levels.solution:
SELECT artist, COUNT(*) AS song_count, AVG(spotify_streams) AS avg_streams
FROM top_songs
WHERE release_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
GROUP BY artist
ORDER BY song_count DESC, artist;
levels.hintMessage: BETWEEN includes both end dates. After filtering, GROUP BY artist so COUNT and AVG run per artist.
levels.successMessage: Great work! You combined a date range filter with two aggregates and a group—that's real reporting SQL.
